meta.title: NCLEX Practice — Evidence-Based Practice (NR449) Week 1
meta.subtitle: Week 1 · Intro to EBP · Research as Evidence · Historical Events · Ethics · Research & the Law · 28 items
meta.footnote: NR449 Week 1 practice · 28 items · rationale after each answer
meta.cardTitle: Week 1 Quiz — EBP Foundations, Research Ethics & Law

questions.stem:
On a telemetry unit, five nurses each handle new-onset hypoglycemia differently: two give juice first, two page the provider first, and one rechecks the glucose in 30 minutes before acting.
The unit council reviews the research and builds an evidence-based hypoglycemia order set and algorithm.
Which result does the council expect this tool to produce?
opts: Consistent practice among the nurses, with reduced variability in how care is given
A foundation for safe care that no longer rests on unit tradition and habit
Accountability to the client, who is the consumer of the care being delivered
Assessment findings and nursing diagnoses tailored to each client's unique condition
questions.rat: The guide lists order sets and algorithms under client management tools, whose stated purpose is to encourage consistent practice and reduce variability. Individualized assessment and nursing diagnoses belong to nursing care processes, accountability to the client belongs to evidence as the basis for client care, and replacing 'how things have always been done' describes policies and procedures.
questions.strat: Order set or algorithm = standardize the many into one; ask which of the four uses of evidence the tool itself serves.
questions.why: Order sets and algorithms are the guide's client management tools, and their stated purpose is to encourage consistent practice and reduce variability among providers. The hypoglycemia algorithm exists to standardize the five nurses' differing responses into one evidence-based pathway that every nurse follows the same way.
whyNot: This describes policies and procedures replacing tradition with an evidence-based foundation for care, a different category from the client-management tool tested here.
Accountability to the client as care's consumer is evidence functioning as the basis for client care, not a client-management tool like an order set.
Individualized assessment findings and nursing diagnoses describe nursing care processes, the opposite of the standardized, one-size approach an algorithm is built to produce.

questions.stem:
A baccalaureate-prepared staff nurse tells the unit educator she wants to practice from current evidence but cannot: her assignment leaves no time to review new literature, the statistical terminology in the articles she does find is confusing, and she does not know how to search the hospital's databases.
Which actions should the educator recommend? Select all that apply.
opts: Wait until she is enrolled in a graduate program to begin appraising evidence
Sign up for email alerts from nursing journals and join a professional organization
Ask the unit council to purchase individual articles from journal publishers
Contact the hospital librarian, who can assist with database searches remotely
Join the unit's journal club, which works through research terminology together
Adopt the practices used by the most experienced nurses on the unit
questions.rat: The guide pairs each barrier with a specific solution: no time to review evidence is met with journal email subscriptions and professional organizations, difficulty with statistical and research terminology is met with a journal club, and lack of database access is met with a staff educator or local librarian, who can often help remotely. Delaying appraisal until graduate school contradicts the baccalaureate role of participating on research teams and applying evidence; buying articles and copying senior nurses' habits address neither barrier and return practice to custom and tradition.
questions.strat: Match the barrier to its named solution: no time to journals, no understanding to journal club, no access to the librarian.
questions.why: The guide pairs each barrier with a named solution. No time to review evidence is met with journal email alerts and professional organizations. Confusing statistical terminology is met with a journal club. Lack of database access is met with the hospital librarian, who can often help remotely.
whyNot: Delaying appraisal until graduate school contradicts the baccalaureate-level expectation to participate on research teams and apply evidence now.
Purchasing individual articles addresses neither named barrier and is not a solution the guide pairs with any of them.
Copying senior nurses' habits returns practice to custom and tradition instead of addressing any of the three named barriers.

questions.stem:
On an orthopedic unit, nurses remove the surgical dressing at 24 hours because, as the preceptor explains, the unit has always done it that way and the incisions seem to heal fine.
A nurse who questions the routine gathers information to decide whether the practice should continue.
Which source of knowledge should carry the most weight in that decision?
opts: Chart audit data on the unit's surgical site infection rates over two quarters
The clinical judgment of the nurses who have worked on this unit the longest
A wound care blog written by a client who healed well after early removal
Published research studies on dressing removal timing and wound outcomes
questions.rat: In the CASTLE framework, scientific research is named the most objective source of nursing knowledge. Assembled information from chart audits is legitimate quality improvement data but is limited to this organization; relying on senior nurses is customs and tradition plus trial and error, which the guide warns may not be best for the client; and an expert source should be authored by a nurse or other provider rather than a lay person.
questions.strat: CASTLE: only the S is called the most objective. Tradition, trial and error, and lay authors are the traps.
questions.why: In the CASTLE framework, scientific research is named the most objective source of nursing knowledge. It comes from rigorous, systematic study rather than personal experience or opinion. Because this question concerns client safety, published studies on dressing-removal timing and wound outcomes should carry the most weight.
whyNot: Chart audit data is assembled information, a legitimate quality-improvement source, but it is limited to this one unit.
Relying on the longest-tenured nurses' judgment reflects customs and tradition plus trial and error, sources the guide warns may not serve the client best.
An expert source should be authored by a nurse or provider. A client's personal blog is a lay account, not a credible authority.

questions.stem:
A hospital is forming an evidence-based practice council and needs nurses at several preparation levels.
Match each contribution the council needs with the level of nursing education that typically prepares a nurse to provide it.

rows.t: Serves as a team member and applies published evidence at the bedside
Conducts a study independently and seeks grant funding to finance it
Writes the facility's EBP guidelines and leads the team's ongoing EBP discussions
Tailors analyzed data to this unit's client population and partners with research scientists

questions.rat: The guide's education table assigns the baccalaureate nurse to understanding EBP basics, participating on research teams, and applying evidence; the master's nurse to creating EBP guidelines and leading teams that discuss EBP; the practice-focused doctorate to analyzing data, tailoring it to specific groups, and partnering with research scientists using advanced leadership; and the research-focused doctorate to conducting research independently and seeking grants. Students commonly credit the master's nurse with independent research or assume the bedside nurse has no role at all.
questions.strat: Climb the ladder: apply, then guide, then translate for a population, then generate. Grant writing is the research doctorate's tell.
questions.why: The guide's education table assigns each level a distinct role. The baccalaureate nurse understands EBP basics, participates on research teams, and applies published evidence at the bedside. The master's nurse writes EBP guidelines and leads teams discussing them. The practice-focused doctorate analyzes data, tailors it to a population, and partners with research scientists. The research-focused doctorate conducts independent studies and seeks grant funding.

questions.stem:
A journal club reads one small study reporting that a revised turning schedule lowered pressure injury rates on a single unit.
Members disagree about whether that is enough to change their own turning protocol.
Which factor best supports going ahead with the practice change?
opts: The authors' names were withheld from the experts who evaluated the manuscript
The study ran in a journal that several council members already subscribe to
Later studies using the same schedule reported similar reductions in injuries
The facility holds Magnet designation and expects bedside nurses to lead change
questions.rat: The guide defines replication as a repeated study with results similar to a prior study, which is what makes nurses confident enough to consider a practice change. Blinded review only removes reviewer bias about the author, journal familiarity says nothing about the strength of the findings, and Magnet designation reflects an organization's commitment to EBP rather than evidence that this particular change works.
questions.strat: One study is a signal; a repeated study is a reason. Look for replication before changing a protocol.
questions.why: Replication means a repeated study reports results similar to a prior study. The guide says this repetition is what gives nurses enough confidence to consider a practice change. Because later studies reproduced the same reduction in pressure injuries, this finding no longer rests on one small study alone.
whyNot: Blinded review only removes reviewer bias about who wrote the study. It says nothing about whether the finding itself has held up.
Being a journal the council already subscribes to says nothing about the strength of this particular study's findings.
Magnet designation reflects the organization's overall commitment to evidence-based practice, not evidence that this specific turning schedule works.

questions.stem:
A unit practice council is deciding whether to change its intramuscular injection technique. Four articles are on the table:
Article A — a report pooling several randomized controlled trials with large samples and large effect sizes
Article B — one randomized controlled study with a small sample and several limitations stated by the authors
Article C — a cohort study comparing two intact groups of nurses, with no randomization
Article D — a chart review presented alongside two expert opinion papers
Which article supports the strongest recommendation for or against the change?
opts: Article A — pooled randomized trials support the strongest recommendation
Article D — expert opinion captures the current consensus at the bedside
Article B — one randomized trial rules out bias better than pooled findings
Article C — intact-group comparisons best reflect actual nursing units
questions.rat: The guide grades evidence by study design: Level I is multiple RCTs with large samples and large effect sizes, and the strength table pairs RCTs or reports of multiple RCTs with a strong recommendation to use or not use the findings. Article B is an RCT with limitations, which only rates "recommend"; Article C is Level III non-randomized intact-group evidence; Article D is Level IV chart review and expert opinion, where the guide says action is optional.
questions.strat: Name the design first, then read its row off the strength table — pooled RCTs are the only "strong" row.
questions.why: The guide grades evidence by study design, and Level I is multiple randomized controlled trials with large samples and large effect sizes. The strength table pairs pooled RCTs with a strong recommendation to use or not use the findings, which is the only row rated that strongly.
whyNot: Article D is chart review and expert opinion, the guide's Level IV, where the strength table marks action as optional rather than a strong recommendation.
Article B is a single randomized trial with stated limitations, which the strength table rates only as recommend, not strong.
Article C is Level III evidence from a non-randomized comparison of intact groups, a weaker design than pooled trials.

questions.stem: A nurse is appraising articles gathered for a proposed practice change. Classify each feature of the articles as supporting credibility or raising a credibility concern.

rows.t: The authors list their professional degrees and years of experience in the specialty
The study was conducted and published eight years ago
A reviewer with no connection to the authors completed a blind peer review
The lead researcher is paid by the company that manufactures the studied product
A separate research team repeated the study and obtained the same results
Two members of the journal's editorial board hold a financial stake in the study

questions.rat: The guide's appraisal checklist asks whether the source is credible (disclosed degrees and experience mark subject matter expertise), whether a neutral party unconnected to the authors performed a blind peer review, and whether the study has been replicated, since reproduced results make findings more generalizable and raise validity. It raises concerns when evidence falls outside the last 3–5 years, or when either the researcher or the editorial board stands to gain financially.
questions.strat: Credible = credentials, blind review, replication, published within 3–5 years; concern = anyone with money riding on the result.
questions.why: The appraisal checklist rewards disclosed credentials, since these establish subject-matter expertise. It also rewards a blind peer review by a neutral party unconnected to the authors. Replication by an independent team counts too, since reproduced results raise validity and generalizability. The checklist flags evidence older than 3–5 years and any financial stake held by the researcher or the editorial board.

questions.stem: A baccalaureate-prepared nurse is asked to lead a review of the unit's medication administration practice after a rise in error reports. Which actions fit the nurse's role and the process for building an evidence-based change? Select all that apply.
opts: Include qualitative studies describing client satisfaction and treatment burden
Set aside the client preference data, since only quantitative results are evidence
Weigh consensus statements from expert practice panels alongside study findings
Use appraised research-based evidence to solve the identified practice problem
Keep the current method, since the unit has used it for years without complaint
Screen each article for financial ties held by the researcher or editorial board
questions.rat: Evidence-based nursing combines the best scientific evidence with clinical experience (expert panels, practice groups, consensus statements) and patient preferences, which the guide measures through satisfaction, quality of life, treatment burden, and qualitative studies; appraisal includes confirming the researcher has nothing to gain. The guide also states that the baccalaureate-prepared nurse is expected to utilize research-based evidence to solve practice problems. Continuing a method because it is long-standing is exactly what research exists to challenge, and client preference is one of the three legs of the triad, not an optional add-on.
questions.strat: Three legs — science, clinician experience, client preference. An option that amputates a leg is wrong.
questions.why: Evidence-based nursing combines the best scientific evidence with clinical experience, such as expert panels and consensus statements, and with patient preferences. The guide measures preference through satisfaction, treatment burden, and qualitative studies. Appraisal also requires confirming researchers have nothing to gain. The guide expects the baccalaureate nurse to use appraised research-based evidence to solve identified practice problems.
whyNot: Client preference is one of the triad's three legs, not data to set aside just because it is not quantitative.
Continuing a method because the unit has used it for years is exactly the custom-and-tradition thinking evidence-based review exists to challenge.

questions.stem:
Three situations reach the unit council in the same month. Using the categories the guide gives for uncovering a need for evidence-based practice, classify each one.

Medication error reports, client concerns, and nurse observations all point to a rise in errors: [1].
The Centers for Disease Control publishes a new catheter-associated urinary tract infection protocol: [2].
The facility is offered a trial of a medication dispensing machine that just came to market: [3].

blanks.label: [1] Rise in medication errors
opts: New equipment, technology, and products
Problem-focused
Nursing knowledge

blanks.label: [2] New CDC CAUTI protocol
opts: Problem-focused
New equipment, technology, and products
Nursing knowledge

blanks.label: [3] Medication dispensing machine
opts: Problem-focused
Nursing knowledge
New equipment, technology, and products

questions.rat: The guide names three categories of factors that uncover a need to study something: problem-focused (error reports, client concerns, nurse observations), nursing knowledge (the newly published CDC CAUTI protocol), and new equipment, technology, and products (the new dispensing machine). Students commonly file the CAUTI protocol as problem-focused because infection is a problem, but nothing on the unit flagged it — the trigger was newly published knowledge.
questions.strat: Ask what triggered the question: our own data (problem), someone else's new publication (knowledge), or a new product on the market.
questions.why: The guide names three triggers for identifying a need. Problem-focused issues come from error reports, client concerns, and nurse observations. New nursing knowledge means a freshly published protocol or guideline. New equipment, technology, or products means something newly available on the market. The CAUTI protocol counts as nursing knowledge because nothing on the unit flagged the issue. A national body simply published new guidance.

questions.stem: A nurse on a pediatric medical-surgical unit finds a report pooling randomized controlled trials of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection prevention bundle. Every trial enrolled adults in intensive care units. The nurse is deciding whether these findings should drive a practice change on her unit. Which judgment is best supported?
opts: Level I evidence is the strongest grade, so the bundle can be applied to any population
External validity is unclear here — adult ICU findings may not transfer to her clients
The bundle is ready to adopt once she confirms the trials were peer reviewed and recent
The report is unusable, because studies run on her own unit are the only valid guide
questions.rat: The guide requires that research applied to practice meet the clients' needs, be assessed for credibility, and have external validity — the ability to generalize findings to other groups of people, locations, and situations. The level of evidence grades the strength of the design, not its fit to a different population, so a Level I report does not license automatic transfer to pediatric clients. Peer review and recency are credibility checks that leave the population mismatch unaddressed, and rejecting all research not conducted on one's own unit would make evidence-based practice impossible.
questions.strat: Level tells you how strong the study is; external validity tells you whether it is about your patients. Both have to clear.
questions.why: Applying research to practice requires meeting the clients' needs, appraising credibility, and confirming external validity. External validity is the ability to generalize findings to other groups, locations, and situations. Because every trial enrolled adult ICU patients, the bundle's fit to pediatric clients is genuinely unclear no matter how strong the evidence grade is.
whyNot: The level of evidence grades how strong a study's design is, not whether its population matches a different group of clients.
Peer review and recency are credibility checks. Neither one addresses whether adult ICU findings transfer to a pediatric population.
Rejecting every study not conducted on her own unit would make evidence-based practice impossible, since almost no research is unit-specific.

questions.stem:
A nursing student reviews the Willowbrook Study for a class discussion. Children with learning disabilities living at a state-run school were purposely exposed to hepatitis and observed while untreated. Enrollment at the school was closed, but children whose parents agreed to let them take part in the study were admitted.

Which Belmont Report principle does the admission arrangement most directly violate?
opts: Beneficence, because deliberate exposure to hepatitis subjected the children to harm
Nonmaleficence, because treatment was withheld from the children who became infected
Justice, because institutionalized children bore the burdens of the research
Respect for persons, because consent was pressured by the offer of admission
questions.rat: Respect for persons rests on autonomy and protection of vulnerable populations: consent must be voluntary and free of coercion, and tying school admission to study participation is the element of influence the guide describes. Beneficence (harm and benefit) and justice (fair distribution of burdens) were also violated by the study overall, but the admission arrangement specifically attacks voluntary consent; nonmaleficence is not one of the three Belmont principles.
questions.strat: Belmont has exactly three: beneficence, justice, respect for persons. Anything about consent, coercion, or a vulnerable group lands on respect for persons.
questions.why: Respect for persons rests on autonomy and protection of vulnerable populations. Consent must be voluntary and free of coercion. Tying school admission to study participation is exactly the added element of influence the guide describes, compromising these children's ability to consent freely.
whyNot: Deliberate hepatitis exposure did violate beneficence by causing harm, but the admission arrangement itself is a consent problem, not a harm-benefit problem.
Nonmaleficence is not one of the Belmont Report's three principles, so it cannot be the one violated here.
Justice concerns fair distribution of burdens across the study overall, but the admission arrangement specifically targets voluntary consent, not distribution.

questions.topic: Events and the Protections They Produced
questions.stem: Match each event or need to the protection or document that followed it. One pool item is not used.
shared: The Nuremberg Code, the first international guidelines on voluntary consent
The Declaration of Helsinki (1964), adopted by the World Medical Association
The National Research Act (1974) and the commission that drafted The Belmont Report
The Common Rule (1981), the Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects
An immediate halt to all gene therapy research at the university involved
The hepatitis vaccine that remains in use today

rows.t: Concentration camp detainees were experimented on without any consent
Men with syphilis went untreated for 40 years and were never told they were subjects
A standard was needed to separate therapeutic from non-therapeutic research
One federal standard was needed for IRB approval and recorded informed consent
Jesse Gelsinger died after a large dose of the study virus

questions.rat: Nazi experimentation led to the Nuremberg Trials and the Nuremberg Code, the first international guidelines on voluntary participation and informed consent. Public outrage over Tuskegee produced the National Research Act of 1974, which created the commission that drafted The Belmont Report. Helsinki, an extension of the Nuremberg Code, drew the therapeutic versus non-therapeutic line; the Common Rule made IRB approval and documented consent law. The Gelsinger death stopped the university's gene therapy research; the hepatitis vaccine came out of Willowbrook, which produced no document.
questions.strat: Follow the chain in order: Nazi to Nuremberg, Tuskegee to Belmont, then the Common Rule turns Belmont's ideas into law.
questions.why: Nazi experimentation led to the Nuremberg Code, the first international guidelines on voluntary consent. Tuskegee's outrage produced the National Research Act of 1974, which created the commission behind The Belmont Report. Helsinki, extending the Nuremberg Code, drew the line between therapeutic and non-therapeutic research. The Common Rule turned IRB approval and documented consent into federal law. Gelsinger's death instead halted only the university's own gene therapy research.

questions.stem:
A nurse serving on a research committee is asked to identify which requirements come from The Nuremberg Code itself rather than from a later document.

Which requirements belong to The Nuremberg Code? Select all that apply.
opts: Human experiments should be based on previous animal experimentation
Research institutions must comply with federal policy and keep review records
A subject may end participation in the experiment at any point
A legally authorized representative may consent for a cognitively impaired subject
An Institutional Review Board must approve the protocol before subjects enroll
The risks of the experiment should not exceed its benefits
questions.rat: The Code's ten principles include grounding human trials in prior animal work, a subject's right to end participation at any time, and risks that never exceed benefits. Surrogate consent for a minor or cognitively impaired subject comes from the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki; mandatory IRB approval and institutional compliance with recordkeeping come from The Belmont Report and the Common Rule, which arrived decades later.
questions.strat: Nuremberg is about the subject and the investigator; IRBs and institutional paperwork are later American additions.
questions.why: The Nuremberg Code's ten principles require that human experiments be grounded in prior animal work. They also require that a subject may end participation at any point, and that the risks of an experiment never exceed its benefits. These three requirements come directly from the Code's original 1947 text, decades before any American regulatory document existed.
whyNot: Institutional compliance with federal policy and recordkeeping requirements comes from the Common Rule of 1981, decades after Nuremberg.
Surrogate consent for a cognitively impaired subject was introduced by the 2013 revision of the Declaration of Helsinki, not the original Code.
Mandatory IRB approval traces to The Belmont Report and the Common Rule, American institutions built decades after the Code was written.

questions.stem:
A nurse researcher is preparing five proposals for the Institutional Review Board.

Classify the level of IRB review each proposal requires.

rows.t: A survey of staff nurses about shift preferences that poses no risk
A federally funded trial of an experimental drug, with publication planned
A walking protocol whose discomfort is no greater than that of daily life
Data pulled from existing medical records, with no contact with clients
A wound dressing trial carrying more than minimal risk of skin injury

questions.rat: Exempt review covers studies posing no risk to subjects, such as surveys or chart data, though the researcher still follows ethical principles. Expedited review, done by one or two members, fits minimal-risk studies in which discomfort is no greater than daily life. Full committee review is required when risk exceeds minimal; these studies often carry federal funding and anticipate publication, so consent, data collection, and subject selection are inspected closely.
questions.strat: Sort by risk: no risk is exempt, everyday-life risk is expedited, more than minimal risk goes to the full committee.
questions.why: Exempt review covers studies posing no risk, such as surveys or existing chart data, though the researcher must still follow ethical principles. Expedited review, completed by one or two members, fits minimal-risk studies where discomfort is no greater than daily life. Full committee review is required once risk exceeds minimal, typically when federal funding and planned publication are involved.

questions.stem:
A nurse reviews a proposal to test an investigational drug on adults with advanced cancer who may benefit from receiving it.

By the definitions in this lesson, the proposal is [1]. The document that drew this distinction is [2]. If the investigators later ask to enroll children instead, that change is acceptable when [3].

blanks.label: [1] Type of research
opts: therapeutic research
exempt research
non-therapeutic research

blanks.label: [2] Source document
opts: The Declaration of Helsinki
The Nuremberg Code
The Belmont Report

blanks.label: [3] Condition for enrolling children
opts: the Institutional Review Board classifies the protocol as an expedited review
the study promotes the health of that population and cannot be done in competent adults
the parents provide written permission before any study procedures begin

questions.rat: Therapeutic research offers the subject a chance at beneficial treatment, while non-therapeutic research seeks knowledge without benefiting the subject; the Declaration of Helsinki, an extension of the Nuremberg Code, was written to draw that line. Helsinki permits surrogate consent for minors, but it also holds that vulnerable populations may be studied only when the work promotes that population's health and cannot be done in competent adults, so parental permission alone or an expedited classification does not justify the switch.
questions.strat: Ask who benefits: the subject means therapeutic. For a vulnerable group, permission is not enough; the need for that group has to be justified.
questions.why: Therapeutic research offers subjects a chance at beneficial treatment. Non-therapeutic research seeks knowledge without benefiting the subject, and the Declaration of Helsinki was written to draw that line. Helsinki permits surrogate consent for minors. A vulnerable population may be studied only when the work promotes that population's health and cannot be done in competent adults. Parental permission or an expedited classification alone does not meet that bar.

questions.stem:
A genetically engineered cold virus previously tested only in animals was used to deliver genes correcting a genetic liver disorder. The Institutional Review Board approved the study, and the subjects were stable adults with that disorder. Jesse Gelsinger, an 18-year-old, was enrolled next to last despite reports raising concern about the safety of the virus, received a dose far larger than the first subject's, and died of a massive immune response.

Which conclusion does this case best support?
opts: Gene therapy protocols are safe for human subjects once an institutional review board approves them
Stable adult subjects carry the same research risk as subjects who are acutely ill
IRB approval does not relieve investigators of the duty to act on new safety reports
An 18-year-old cannot consent to research without a parent's signature on the form
questions.rat: The case turned on whether high-risk research belongs in healthy, stable clients and whether adverse-event reports were ignored or misinterpreted, so IRB approval at the start does not end the investigator's obligation to respond to accumulating safety data. Approval is not a safety guarantee, stable subjects were the point of contention rather than an equivalence to acutely ill ones, and at 18 the subject could consent for himself.
questions.strat: IRB approval is a starting gate, not a finish line; new safety data reopens the question.
questions.why: The Gelsinger case turned on whether high-risk research belongs in healthy, stable clients, and whether investigators ignored or misinterpreted mounting adverse-event reports. IRB approval at the study's start did not end the team's obligation to respond to new safety data. Reports had already raised concern about the virus before Gelsinger was enrolled.
whyNot: IRB approval is a starting requirement, not a guarantee of safety, so it does not make gene therapy protocols inherently safe.
Whether stable subjects carry the same risk as acutely ill ones was the case's central controversy, not an established equivalence.
At eighteen, Gelsinger was a legal adult who could consent to research for himself, without a parent's signature.

questions.stem:
A nurse researcher studying burnout recruits staff from her own unit. At the staff meeting she announces that taking part will be noted in each nurse's annual performance evaluation, and that she will tell the manager which nurses decline.

Which participant right is the researcher violating?
opts: The right to self-determination — participation must be free of coercion
The right to full disclosure — the study's risks must be described first
The right to privacy — the data provided must be held in strict confidence
The right to fair treatment — selection must rest on study requirements
questions.rat: Coercion is an explicit or implicit threat of penalty for failing to participate, or an excessive reward for agreeing. Tying enrollment to a performance evaluation and reporting refusers to the manager is a threat of penalty, so it violates the right to self-determination under respect for human dignity. Full disclosure governs what the participant is told about the study, fair treatment governs how participants are selected and treated, and privacy governs how their data are handled — none is the breach described here.
questions.strat: A penalty for saying no, or a payout too large to refuse — both are coercion, and both hit self-determination.
questions.why: Coercion is an explicit or implicit threat of penalty for not participating, or an excessive reward for agreeing to take part. Tying enrollment to a performance evaluation, and reporting who declined to the manager, is a threat of penalty. That violates the right to self-determination under respect for human dignity.
whyNot: Full disclosure governs what participants are told about study risks and benefits, a separate right from the coercion described here.
The right to privacy governs how participants' data are handled, not how they are pressured to enroll in the first place.
Fair treatment governs how participants are selected and treated, not the threat of an unfavorable evaluation for declining.

questions.stem:
A consent form for a wound-care trial describes the study's purpose, the procedures, and how to reach the researcher. It does not mention that the experimental dressing may cause skin irritation, and it does not state that the client may decline to take part. The client signs the form.

How should the nurse evaluate this consent?
opts: It is not valid; a consent form must be witnessed by a second researcher
It is not valid; disclosure must include risks and the right to refuse
It is valid; a description of the procedures satisfies the disclosure rule
It is valid; the signed form is evidence that participation was voluntary
questions.rat: Informed consent rests on two elements: the right to self-determination and the right to full disclosure. Full disclosure means the researcher has fully described the study, the person's right to refuse participation, and the potential risks and benefits — this form omits both the risk of irritation and the right to refuse, so the signature does not make the consent valid. A second witness is not the element the guide names, and describing procedures alone falls short of full disclosure.
questions.strat: Informed consent = self-determination + full disclosure; if either leg is missing, a signature does not rescue it.
questions.why: Informed consent rests on two elements: self-determination and full disclosure. Full disclosure means describing the study, the right to refuse, and the risks and benefits. This form omits both the risk of skin irritation and the right to refuse, so a signature alone cannot make this consent valid.
whyNot: A second researcher's witness signature is not one of the two elements the guide requires for valid consent.
Describing the procedures alone falls short of full disclosure, which also requires stating the risks and the right to refuse.
A signature only shows the client signed. It cannot substitute for the risk and refusal information the form never disclosed.

questions.stem:
The Belmont Report articulated three primary ethical principles for research with human participants.

Match each researcher action to the principle it upholds.

rows.t: Enrolling women and members of minority groups rather than excluding them from a clinical trial
Holding the interview recordings in strict confidence in line with the HIPAA Privacy Rule
Assuring participants that what they report about their income will not cost them public benefits
Describing the study, its risks and benefits, and the right to refuse before asking for a signature
Telling participants they may skip any question or drop out of the study at any point
Rewording an interview guide so bereaved parents are not put through unnecessary emotional distress

questions.rat: Beneficence obliges the researcher to minimize harm and maximize benefit; it carries both the right to freedom from harm and discomfort (which includes emotional harm) and the right to protection from exploitation (what participants disclose must not be used against them). Respect for human dignity carries self-determination (refuse, skip questions, withdraw) and full disclosure (the study, its risks and benefits, and the right to refuse). Justice carries the right to fair treatment (equitable selection, no exclusion of women and minorities) and the right to privacy (data held in strict confidence, HIPAA).
questions.strat: Beneficence = protect them; human dignity = tell them and let them choose; justice = treat them fairly and guard their data.
questions.why: Beneficence obliges researchers to minimize harm and maximize benefit, covering freedom from harm and discomfort, including emotional harm, and protection from exploitation of disclosed information. Respect for human dignity covers self-determination, refusing, skipping questions, withdrawing, and full disclosure of the study, its risks and benefits, and the right to refuse. Justice covers fair treatment, equitable selection without excluding groups, and privacy of the data participants provide.

questions.stem:
A nurse is enrolling clients from her own clinic panel into a study of a new diabetes education program.

Which actions by the nurse uphold the participants' right to self-determination? Select all that apply.
opts: Offer clients on public assistance a $500 payment to encourage them to enroll
Answer the client's questions about the study before asking for a signature
Enroll clients who seem agreeable and go over the study details at the next visit
Tell each client she may refuse to answer any question during the interviews
Explain that a client may withdraw from the study at any point after enrolling
State that declining to enroll will not change the care the client receives
questions.rat: Self-determination means prospective participants decide voluntarily, without risking prejudicial treatment, and it includes the right to ask questions, to refuse to answer questions, and to drop out of the study — so refusing individual questions, withdrawing, having questions answered before signing, and knowing that care is unaffected by declining all uphold it. A generous stipend directed at a low-income group is considered mildly coercive because the incentive functions as pressure, and enrolling first while explaining later removes the informed, voluntary decision this principle protects.
questions.strat: Voluntary means the client can say no, say nothing, or stop later — and nothing bad happens either way.
questions.why: Self-determination means prospective participants decide voluntarily, without risking prejudicial treatment, including the right to ask questions, refuse to answer questions, and withdraw at any point. Answering questions before signing, allowing refusal of individual questions, permitting withdrawal, and confirming that declining will not affect care all protect that voluntary choice.
whyNot: A large stipend aimed at a low-income group is considered mildly coercive, since the incentive itself functions as pressure to agree.
Enrolling first and explaining details later removes the informed, voluntary decision self-determination is meant to protect.

questions.stem:
During an in-depth qualitative interview about how parents cope when a child has a terminal illness, a mother begins to cry, says the questions are pulling her back into the worst weeks of her life, and asks how much longer this will take.

Which obligation does this situation place on the researcher?
opts: Justice — the researcher must honor every agreement made with the mother
Fair treatment — the researcher must show respect for the mother's beliefs
Beneficence — the researcher must minimize emotional harm and discomfort
Full disclosure — the researcher must restate the study's aims and risks
questions.rat: Beneficence imposes a duty to minimize harm and maximize benefits, and the guide states that harm and discomfort in research may be physical, emotional (such as stress), social, or financial. Qualitative studies probe highly personal areas, so the researcher must stay aware of the intrusion on the participant's psyche and act to limit it. Honoring agreements and respecting beliefs belong to justice and the right to fair treatment, and full disclosure concerns what she was told before consenting — neither addresses the distress happening now.
questions.strat: Research harm is physical, emotional, social, or financial — tears count, and beneficence owns them.
questions.why: Beneficence imposes a duty to minimize harm and maximize benefit, and harm and discomfort in research may be physical, emotional, social, or financial. Qualitative interviews probe highly personal territory, so when this mother's distress surfaces mid-interview, the researcher must recognize the emotional harm and act to limit it.
whyNot: Justice concerns honoring agreements made with participants, a different obligation from responding to distress happening in the moment.
Fair treatment concerns respecting a participant's beliefs, not the emotional intrusion this line of questioning is causing right now.
Full disclosure concerns what she was told before consenting, which does not address the distress she is experiencing during the interview.

questions.stem:
A researcher studying substance misuse among high school students describes the project to them as a study of student health practices. The students know they are enrolled in a study, and data collection is otherwise open.

Which statements about this practice are accurate? Select all that apply.
opts: It is exempt from the consent requirement because the students are minors
It meets full disclosure, since the description of the study is broadly true
It is concealment, since data are gathered without the students' knowledge
Some hold that it is acceptable when risk is minimal and society benefits
It is deception, since the students are given misinformation about the study
It interferes with the students' ability to make a truly informed decision
questions.rat: Describing a drug-use study as a study of student health practices is what the guide calls a mild form of misinformation, which is deception; both deception and concealment are ethically problematic because they interfere with people's right to make truly informed decisions about the personal costs and benefits of participation. The guide also notes the split view that deception may be acceptable when a study carries minimal risk yet offers benefits to society. Concealment is a different technique — collecting data without participants' knowledge and therefore without consent — and a partly true description does not amount to full disclosure.
questions.strat: Concealment hides the watching; deception distorts the telling. Either one dents informed consent.
questions.why: Describing a drug-use study as a study of student health practices is a mild form of misinformation, which the guide defines as deception. Deception is ethically problematic because it interferes with a person's right to make a truly informed decision about the costs and benefits of taking part. Some hold that it is acceptable when risk is minimal and society benefits.
whyNot: Being minors does not exempt a study from consent requirements. Vulnerable populations need more protection, not less.
A partly true description does not amount to full disclosure, which requires accurately describing the actual study being conducted.
This is deception, not concealment. Students know they are enrolled in a study, so nothing is being hidden from them.

questions.stem:
A team designing a study of a sleep intervention plans to enroll only men in a state prison, explaining that this group is easy to reach, unlikely to move away, and available for repeat measurements. Nothing about the intervention itself is specific to incarcerated men.

Which right does this recruitment plan violate?
opts: The right to fair treatment — selection must follow the study's requirements
The right to freedom from harm — the sleep protocol may cause them discomfort
The right to self-determination — the men were offered no payment to take part
The right to protection from exploitation — their data may be used against them
questions.rat: Justice includes the right to fair treatment, which calls for equitable distribution of the benefits and burdens of research and requires that participants be selected on the basis of research requirements rather than their vulnerabilities. The guide names prisoners as an example of a group of lower social standing chosen for convenience, which is precisely this scenario. Protection from exploitation (part of beneficence) would apply if what participants disclosed were used against them, freedom from harm concerns risk of injury or distress, and self-determination concerns voluntary consent — no payment is required, and an excessive one would itself be coercive.
questions.strat: Ask why this group: if the answer is convenience rather than the science, the problem is justice.
questions.why: The right to fair treatment calls for equitable distribution of research's burdens and requires selecting participants based on study requirements, not their vulnerabilities. The guide names prisoners as an example of a group of lower social standing chosen for convenience, which is exactly this recruitment plan.
whyNot: Freedom from harm concerns injury or distress from the protocol itself, not why this particular group was chosen to receive it.
Self-determination concerns voluntary consent. No payment is required, and an excessive one would itself raise coercion concerns.
Protection from exploitation applies when disclosed information could be used against participants, not when a group is chosen for convenience.

questions.stem:
A nurse researcher is recruiting clients from a cardiology clinic. To speed enrollment, the researcher e-mails a list of clients' names, diagnoses, and phone numbers to a nurse at an unaffiliated hospital who is not part of the study team.

The regulation the researcher has violated is the module's example of which category of law?
opts: Common law, which is derived from custom and judicial precedent
Tort law, which covers an act or omission that causes harm to another
Statutory law, which consists of acts passed by the United States Congress
Administrative law, which regulates government agencies and their rules
questions.rat: The module lists the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) as its example of administrative law — the laws and legal principles governing the creation, administration, and regulation of government agencies. Statutory law is the module's Medicare/Medicaid example (acts of Congress), common law is its medical malpractice example (custom and precedent), and tort is its defective-instrument example (an act or omission causing harm).
questions.strat: Match each of the four law categories to the module's own example: malpractice = common, HIPAA = administrative, Medicare/Medicaid = statutory, defective instrument = tort.
questions.why: The module lists HIPAA as its example of administrative law, the laws and legal principles governing the creation, administration, and regulation of government agencies. E-mailing client names, diagnoses, and phone numbers to someone outside the study team without authorization is exactly the kind of HIPAA violation this category covers.
whyNot: The module's example of common law is medical malpractice, which rests on custom and judicial precedent, not a HIPAA data breach.
The module's example of tort law is using a known defective instrument, an act causing harm rather than a records disclosure.
The module's example of statutory law is Medicare and Medicaid, acts passed by Congress rather than agency regulations like HIPAA.

questions.stem:
A nurse serving on an Institutional Review Board is sorting new proposals into the level of review each one requires.

Classify each proposal.

rows.t: Participants walk on a treadmill for 10 minutes; discomfort is no greater than that of daily life
An anonymous survey of staff nurses about shift-scheduling preferences
A federally funded trial of an investigational wound dressing that carries a risk of skin injury
One extra tube of blood is drawn during an already scheduled venipuncture
A retrospective chart review of hemoglobin A1c values with no client contact
A trial of a new sedation protocol in critically ill adults, with findings submitted for publication

questions.rat: Exempt review covers studies that pose no risk, such as surveys or data collected from medical records; the researcher still must adhere to ethical principles. Expedited review applies when risk is minimal — the probability of physical or emotional discomfort is no greater than that experienced in daily life — and one or two IRB members approve or deny it. Full review by the entire committee is required when risk is more than minimal, and is typical where federal funds are received and publication is anticipated.
questions.strat: Sort by risk, not by topic: no risk = exempt, no worse than daily life = expedited, more than minimal risk (often federally funded) = full committee.
questions.why: Exempt review covers studies posing no risk, such as anonymous surveys or retrospective chart data with no client contact, though ethical principles still apply. Expedited review fits minimal-risk studies, such as an extra tube of blood or a treadmill walk, where discomfort is no greater than daily life. Full committee review applies once risk is more than minimal, typically with federal funding and planned publication.

questions.stem:
During a study team huddle, a nurse researcher tells the group that one participant "makes up her symptoms to stay enrolled," a claim the researcher knows is untrue. She then repeats that same claim in the written monthly progress report circulated to the funding agency. Separately, a printout of the participant's health information is left on a counter where unit visitors can read it.

Complete the statements.

blanks.label: [1] The remark made during the huddle is
opts: invasion of privacy
libel
defamation

blanks.label: [2] The claim in the circulated report is
opts: invasion of privacy
defamation
libel

blanks.label: [3] The printout left on the counter is
opts: defamation
invasion of privacy
libel

questions.rat: The module defines defamation as a false and harmful oral statement and libel as a false statement that is published or written, so the spoken huddle remark is defamation and the same claim in the circulated report is libel. Subjects also have the right to have their health information kept confidential and released only to authorized individuals, so an exposed printout is a violation of privacy rather than a false statement.
questions.strat: Libel starts like "letter" — written or published; defamation is what is said out loud. Privacy is about who can see the information, not whether it is true.
questions.why: Defamation is a false and harmful oral statement, while libel is a false statement that is published or written. The spoken huddle remark is defamation, and the identical claim in the circulated report is libel. Participants also have the right to have their health information kept confidential, so an exposed printout is a privacy violation rather than a false statement.

questions.stem:
A nurse is auditing the consent process for a study enrolling adults who live at a homeless shelter.

Which findings show that the consent process met the requirements described in the module? Select all that apply.
opts: Participants were given time to review the form before being asked to sign it
The consent form is written in plain language the participants can read and understand
A verbal agreement at the recruiting table was accepted in place of a signature
Participants were told that continued shelter meal service depends on enrolling
The form was rewritten in research terminology so that the wording would be precise
A signed consent form is on file for every enrolled participant
questions.rat: The module sets four requirements: the language must be simple enough to understand, the consent must not be coerced, the consent must be documented, and the subject must have had time to review the document. Tying meal service to enrollment is coercion of a vulnerable population, a verbal yes leaves the consent undocumented, and rewriting the form in research terminology defeats the plain-language requirement.
questions.strat: Four consent checks: understandable, uncoerced, documented, and enough time to review.
questions.why: The module sets four consent requirements: understandable plain language, freedom from coercion, documentation, and enough time to review the form before signing. Giving participants review time and writing the form in plain language each satisfy one requirement. Keeping a signed form on file for every enrolled participant satisfies documentation.
whyNot: A verbal yes at the recruiting table leaves consent undocumented, which fails the documentation requirement regardless of what was discussed.
Tying continued shelter meals to enrollment coerces a vulnerable population, violating the requirement that consent be free of coercion.
Rewriting the form in research terminology defeats the plain-language requirement, even though the wording becomes more technically precise.

questions.stem:
A nurse researcher is conducting a study entirely online. Participants read the informed consent document on a web page and click Submit. The researcher recognizes she cannot observe whether a participant actually read the document, which leaves room for a participant to later claim that consent was not informed.

Which action best addresses this concern?
opts: Require the participant to type their full legal name on the form
E-mail the participant after submission to verify they read the form
Post the consent form on the study web page for any visitor to read
Add a checkbox stating the participant has read and agrees to the form
questions.rat: The module names an e-mail conversation with the participant after they submit the consent document as a way to raise confidence that the participant read and understood the material, and to answer questions or clarify concerns. A checkbox or a typed name records the click but proves nothing about comprehension, and posting the form publicly does not confirm that this participant read it.
questions.strat: Online consent problems are solved by adding a second, two-way contact with the participant, not by adding another click to the form.
questions.why: The module names an e-mail exchange with the participant after they submit the consent form. This raises confidence that they read and understood it, while also giving them a chance to ask questions. This two-way contact directly addresses the concern that online consent cannot be observed as it happens.
whyNot: Typing a full legal name only records a click. It proves nothing about whether the participant actually read and understood the form.
Posting the form publicly for any visitor confirms nothing about whether this specific participant read it before clicking submit.
A checkbox records the click just as a signature would, without verifying actual comprehension of what was read.
